title: UltraFlash: Accelerating Megapixel Visual Synthesis

paper.title: UltraFlash: Accelerating Megapixel Visual Synthesis Thanks: Qualcomm AI Research is an initiative of Qualcomm Technologies, Inc.
paper.abstract: Abstract Megapixel visual synthesis with latent diffusion models requires operating far beyond the resolution at which these models are trained. Cascade refinement is the most successful approach to handling this problem: it upgrades a base image at a regular resolution to the target resolution via multiple cascade upsampling steps, each involving a resolution upgrade traversed through pixel space and a denoising-based refinement in latent space. Although denoising is often treated as the main cost, we identify an underexplored source of overhead: repeatedly moving representations through the VAE. We refer to these steps as pixel-space transitions : intermediate latents are decoded to RGB, resized, and re-encoded before refinement, while final latents are decoded patch by patch with dense overlap to suppress artifacts. We present UltraFlash , which shifts the focus of acceleration from denoising alone to the VAE transitions around it. Its first component, Latent Hyperloop , replaces the intermediate RGB round trip with a learned latent-space shortcut that approximates the same transformation while avoiding repeated VAE calls for decoding and encoding. Its second component, Sparse Patch-based Decoding , makes final reconstruction efficient by tracing patch seams to inconsistent GroupNorm statistics and reusing cached statistics across patches, enabling sparse VAE decoding with much smaller overlap. Integrated into the current state-of-the-art baseline, UltraFlash reduces 4K generation latency by ∼ \sim 2 × \times while improving image quality, demonstrating that transition-level optimization can advance both efficiency and fidelity. More broadly, these transition costs recur across megapixel synthesis pipelines, suggesting that optimizing pixel-space transitions is an effective route to fast, high-fidelity visual synthesis.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Latent diffusion models have greatly advanced visual synthesis, but their native training resolution remains a practical boundary. Although applications increasingly require 2K, 4K, and larger outputs, models trained around 512 × 512 512\times 512 or 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 often produce repeated objects, distorted layouts, or unstable textures when directly evaluated on larger canvases. Fine-tuning on high-resolution data is a natural remedy, but it is difficult to scale: diverse megapixel-scale datasets are limited, training at such resolutions is expensive, and the adapted model often becomes specialized to a fixed target resolution ( Xie et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . Existing alternatives therefore rely on inference-time strategies that reuse pretrained models. Direct extrapolation methods modify inference on enlarged latents, but can suffer from memory cost and structural instability at extreme resolutions. Cascade refinement methods instead generate at a reliable native resolution and progressively construct larger images through refinement stages ( Du et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ; Vontobel et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) . Representative systems differ in how they refine enlarged latents: DemoFusion uses progressive patch-based refinement, FouriScale and FreeScale modify frequency or scale behavior, HiWave uses structure-preserving inversion, and PixelRush ( Lai et al., 2026 ) accelerates the cascade with one-step diffusion refinement. Among these, PixelRush currently provides the strongest speed–quality trade-off, making it the most relevant stress test for remaining non-denoising overhead. We therefore use PixelRush as the main instantiation of UltraFlash, while targeting VAE-heavy pixel-space transitions that are shared by the broader cascade family. Most acceleration efforts for megapixel synthesis focus on denoising or refinement. This is natural, since diffusion sampling is expensive and larger spatial sizes increase the cost of each denoising operation. However, we find that this view is incomplete. Modern cascade pipelines also spend substantial time repeatedly moving representations through the VAE. We call these operations pixel-space transitions : steps where a latent representation is converted to RGB or where RGB is converted back to a latent representation. These transitions appear in two places. First, intermediate latents are often decoded to RGB, resized, and re-encoded before refinement. Second, the final latent must be decoded to RGB, but at megapixel scale this is typically done patch by patch with dense overlap to suppress artifacts. As a result, a significant fraction of runtime is spent not on denoising itself, but on VAE-heavy transitions around denoising. This observation exposes an underexplored source of overhead. The two transitions have different roles and therefore require different solutions. The intermediate RGB round trip is avoidable: it is used as a convenient way to transform a latent before refinement, but it need not be performed through pixels. The final transition is unavoidable because the output image must be RGB, but its dense patch implementation is inefficient. Thus, the design goal is to replace the avoidable intermediate VAE round trip and make the final VAE decoding sparse without introducing seams. We present UltraFlash , which shifts the focus of acceleration from denoising alone to the VAE transitions around it. UltraFlashcontains two components. First, Latent Hyperloop replaces the intermediate RGB round trip with a learned latent-space shortcut. It approximates the decode–resize–encode transformation while avoiding repeated VAE calls for decoding and encoding. Second, Sparse Patch-based Decoding accelerates final reconstruction. We trace sparse patch-decoding artifacts to inconsistent GroupNorm statistics across independently decoded patches. Sparse Patch-based Decoding fixes this by caching normalization statistics from reference patches and reusing them across all patches, enabling sparse VAE decoding with much smaller overlap. Integrated into the current state-of-the-art cascade baseline ( Lai et al., 2026 ) , UltraFlash reduces 4K generation latency by 2 × 2\times while improving image quality. This result shows that VAE transitions remain a substantial optimization spot even in highly optimized megapixel synthesis systems. More broadly, RGB round trips and dense patch-wise VAE decoding appear across cascade pipelines, suggesting that optimizing pixel-space transitions is an effective route to faster, high-fidelity visual synthesis. Our contributions are: • We identify repeated VAE-heavy pixel-space transitions as an underexplored source of overhead in megapixel visual synthesis, beyond denoising and refinement. • We introduce Latent Hyperloop , a learned latent-space shortcut that replaces the intermediate decode–resize–encode round trip while avoiding repeated VAE decoding and encoding. • We introduce Sparse Patch-based Decoding , which enables sparse VAE decoding by sharing cached normalization statistics across independently decoded patches.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Megapixel Visual Synthesis. Scaling diffusion models beyond their native training resolution has been explored through several routes. One route trains or adapts models for native high-resolution generation, such as SANA, HunyuanImage, and other dedicated 2K/4K generators ( Xie et al., 2025 ; Team, 2025 ) . These methods can achieve strong quality, but they require high-resolution data, model adaptation, or dedicated training. A second route directly extrapolates pretrained models to larger canvases through inference-time modifications, such as convolutional dilation ( He et al., 2023 ) , frequency or scale fusion ( Huang et al., 2024 ) , flow-aligned guidance ( Bu et al., 2025 ) , or positional extrapolation for FLUX-based models ( Issachar et al., 2025 ) . These methods avoid retraining, but can suffer from memory cost, structural instability, or unnatural textures at extreme resolutions ( Lin et al., 2024b ) . A third route uses cascade or region-based refinement, synthesizing native-resolution windows and merging them into a larger image through average blending ( Bar-Tal et al., 2023 ; Du et al., 2024 ) , DDIM inversion ( Vontobel et al., 2025 ) , or few-step refinement ( Lai et al., 2026 ) . This cascade line has progressed from multi-step patch refinement in DemoFusion to structure-preserving inversion in HiWave, and most recently to PixelRush, which uses one-step Turbo refinement to deliver the strongest speed–quality trade-off among cascade methods. Our work focuses on the cascade setting because it reuses pretrained models in their reliable operating regime while supporting megapixel outputs. We use PixelRush as the main experimental instantiation because it is already optimized for denoising speed; improving it therefore tests whether VAE transition overhead remains a meaningful bottleneck after the dominant sampling cost has been compressed. Rather than introducing another refinement strategy, UltraFlash optimizes the VAE-heavy transitions surrounding refinement: intermediate RGB round trips that prepare refinement inputs, and final patch-wise VAE decoding that reconstructs the output image. Pixel-Space Transitions. Latent diffusion models use a VAE to move between compressed latents and RGB images ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . In megapixel synthesis, this creates two transition costs. First, intermediate latents are often decoded to RGB, resized, and re-encoded before refinement. This route is stable and avoids artifacts from naive latent manipulation ( Qiu et al., 2025 ; Vontobel et al., 2025 ) , but requires an expensive decode–encode round trip. Because the VAE encoder is nonlinear, ordinary latent interpolation is not that round trip. FAM Diffusion ( Yang et al., 2025 ) compensates with learned frequency and attention modulation over the whole latent, and it changes the denoiser. Latent Hyperloop is a patch-wise shortcut for the same decode–resize–encode transformation and leaves the denoiser unchanged. Second, the final latent must be decoded to RGB. Since full-image VAE decoding is memory-intensive at megapixel scale, pipelines decode overlapping patches and blend them. Large overlaps hide seams but repeat computation; small overlaps reveal boundary artifacts. We identify inconsistent GroupNorm statistics ( Wu and He, 2018 ) across patches as a key cause, and use Sparse Patch-based Decoding to share cached statistics across patches, enabling sparse reconstruction with much smaller overlap. Super-Resolution. Super-resolution methods reconstruct high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs ( Chen et al., 2024b ; Dong et al., 2014 ; Wang et al., 2020 ) . Diffusion-based super-resolution methods ( Li et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) further improve perceptual quality, but are typically trained for restoration. Megapixel visual synthesis differs from restoration: the input is a generated intermediate representation, and the goal is coherent visual synthesis rather than recovering a unique high-resolution target ( Lai et al., 2026 ) . Thus, although super-resolution and megapixel synthesis both involve scale expansion, they address different problem settings and require different evaluation criteria.

sections.text: Latent Diffusion Models ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) perform diffusion in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder. A denoising network ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t ) \epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t) is trained to reverse this process. At inference, a sample is generated by denoising a Gaussian latent and decoding the final latent with the VAE decoder 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . Cascade Refinement Pipelines. Megapixel synthesis commonly starts from the model’s native resolution and progressively enlarges the image through cascade refinement ( Du et al., 2024 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ; Vontobel et al., 2025 ; Lai et al., 2026 ) . Although methods differ in refinement details, each stage typically initializes a larger latent by routing the current latent through RGB. Let 𝐳 0 r \mathbf{z}_{0}^{r} be a clean latent at resolution r r , where a 2 × 2\times increase in height and width maps r r to 4 ​ r 4r . The standard pixel-space transition is 𝐳 ¯ 0 4 ​ r = UP pixel ​ ( 𝐳 0 r ) = ℰ ⁡ ( Interpolate ⁡ ( 𝒟 ⁡ ( 𝐳 0 r ) , 2 ) ) , 𝐳 0 4 ​ r = ϕ ⁡ ( 𝐳 ¯ 0 4 ​ r ) , \bar{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{4r}=\mathrm{UP}_{\mathrm{pixel}}(\mathbf{z}_{0}^{r})=\mathcal{E}\!\left(\mathrm{Interpolate}(\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{z}_{0}^{r}),2)\right),\qquad\mathbf{z}_{0}^{4r}=\phi(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{4r}), (2) where 𝒟 \mathcal{D} and ℰ \mathcal{E} are the VAE decoder and encoder, Interpolate ⁡ ( ⋅ , 2 ) \mathrm{Interpolate}(\cdot,2) resizes the RGB image by 2 × 2\times , and ϕ \phi denotes refinement. This decode–resize–encode route is stable but VAE-heavy. The final latent 𝐳 0 R \mathbf{z}_{0}^{R} must also be decoded to RGB. Since full-image VAE decoding is memory-intensive at megapixel scale, practical systems decode overlapping patches and stitch them together, where dense overlap suppresses seams but repeats computation. Thus, cascade pipelines contain two major transition costs: repeated intermediate VAE round trips and final patch-wise VAE decoding. UltraFlash targets both: Latent Hyperloop replaces the intermediate round trip with a learned latent shortcut, while Sparse Patch-based Decoding makes final reconstruction sparse and consistent.

sections.heading: 4 Accelerating Megapixel Visual Synthesis
sections.text: We present UltraFlash , which shifts acceleration from denoising alone to the VAE-heavy pixel-space transitions that surround it. In cascade megapixel synthesis, these transitions arise twice: intermediate latents undergo an RGB round trip before refinement, while final RGB decoding must be performed patch by patch due to memory constraints. UltraFlash handles these two roles differently: Latent Hyperloop (Sec. 4.1 ) replaces the avoidable intermediate RGB round trip, while Sparse Patch-based Decoding (Sec. 4.2 ) accelerates the unavoidable final decoding. An overview is shown in Fig. 2 .

sections.heading: 4.1 Latent Hyperloop: Bypassing Intermediate RGB Round Trips
sections.text: Figure 2: UltraFlash targets transition costs common to cascade megapixel synthesis. Cascade pipelines often use pixel space twice: an intermediate RGB round trip before refinement and dense patch-wise VAE decoding for final output. UltraFlash accelerates both without changing the denoising/refinement stage. Latent Hyperloop removes repeated VAE decode/encode calls during intermediate transfer, while Sparse Patch-based Decoding reduces final decoding redundancy by enforcing consistent GroupNorm statistics across patches. Motivation. Many cascade refinement pipelines ( Du et al., 2024 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ; Vontobel et al., 2025 ; Lai et al., 2026 ) initialize each refinement stage through a VAE-heavy RGB round trip. Given a latent 𝐳 0 r \mathbf{z}_{0}^{r} , the pipeline decodes it to RGB, changes its spatial scale, and re-encodes the resized image back into latent space: UP pixel ​ ( 𝐳 0 r ) = ℰ ⁡ ( Interpolate ⁡ ( 𝒟 ⁡ ( 𝐳 0 r ) , 2 ) ) , \mathrm{UP}_{\mathrm{pixel}}(\mathbf{z}_{0}^{r})=\mathcal{E}\!\left(\mathrm{Interpolate}(\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{z}_{0}^{r}),2)\right), (3) where 𝒟 \mathcal{D} and ℰ \mathcal{E} denote the VAE decoder and encoder, respectively. The appeal of this RGB round trip is that resizing in pixel space is simple and well-defined. Its drawback is computational cost: each transfer invokes both the VAE decoder and encoder. In our main instantiation with the state-of-the-art cascade method ( Lai et al., 2026 ) , this transition accounts for approximately 30–40% of cascade-stage runtime. The challenge is that the RGB round trip cannot be replaced by ordinary latent interpolation. Since the VAE encoder is nonlinear, spatial resizing in latent space is not equivalent to resizing in RGB and then encoding the result: Interpolate ⁡ ( 𝐳 , 2 ) ≠ ℰ ⁡ ( Interpolate ⁡ ( 𝒟 ⁡ ( 𝐳 ) , 2 ) ) \mathrm{Interpolate}(\mathbf{z},2)\neq\mathcal{E}\!\left(\mathrm{Interpolate}(\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{z}),2)\right) . Thus, we replace generic latent interpolation with a learned latent-space shortcut that approximates the decode–resize–encode transformation while avoiding the VAE decode–encode computation. We define Latent Hyperloop as a lightweight function ℋ ϕ \mathcal{H}_{\phi} that maps the current latent directly to the latent that would otherwise be produced by the RGB round trip: 𝐳 ¯ 0 4 ​ r = ℋ ϕ ​ ( 𝐳 0 r ) ≈ UP pixel ​ ( 𝐳 0 r ) . \bar{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{4r}=\mathcal{H}_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{0}^{r})\approx\mathrm{UP}_{\mathrm{pixel}}(\mathbf{z}_{0}^{r}). (4) Once trained, ℋ ϕ \mathcal{H}_{\phi} replaces the decode–interpolate–encode route during intermediate transfer. A good Latent Hyperloop ℋ ϕ \mathcal{H}_{\phi} must satisfy the following conditions: (1) Accurate in replicating the upsampling operator UP pixel \mathrm{UP}_{\mathrm{pixel}} without going through pixel space, (2) Efficient in both memory usage and computation, causing minimal latency, and (3) General to work at every cascade step. These criteria are challenging, requiring novel designs in data flow, network structure, training data, and training objectives. We will discuss below our proposals to handle each mentioned aspect. Context-Expanded Patching. To make ℋ ϕ \mathcal{H}_{\phi} general and work at every cascade step regardless of input resolution, we design it to process patch-by-patch, using fixed resolutions for the input and output latent patches. Since the follow-up refinement step also processes overlapping patches, a convenient design is to use the same patch configuration in these two steps: the output patches of ℋ ϕ \mathcal{H}_{\phi} should have the same resolution and location as the ones used in the refinement. With that configuration, the patches produced by ℋ ϕ \mathcal{H}_{\phi} can be sent for processing at the refinement step directly, skipping the operation to collect and aggregate them to form the full latent output 𝐳 ¯ 0 4 ​ r \bar{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{4r} . For each target patch in 𝐳 ¯ 0 4 ​ r \bar{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{4r} , a natural input to ℋ ϕ \mathcal{H}_{\phi} is the coordinate-matched source patch in 𝐳 0 r \mathbf{z}_{0}^{r} . However, this crop alone is insufficient. The decode–resize–encode route approximated by ℋ ϕ \mathcal{H}_{\phi} contains convolutional VAE layers, so the target patch depends not only on the aligned source region but also on its surrounding context. We therefore expand each source crop by p p context pixels on every side before feeding it to ℋ ϕ \mathcal{H}_{\phi} , so that a source patch of side length s s becomes an input of side length s + 2 ​ p s+2p ; we use s = 64 s=64 and p = 8 p=8 , i.e., 80 × 80 80\times 80 inputs for 128 × 128 128\times 128 target patches. This context-expanded design captures the local dependencies of the original RGB round trip while preserving patch-wise processing. Its necessity is confirmed by the ablation on p p in Appendix B.2 . Lightweight Spatial Prior. Latent Hyperloop ℋ ϕ \mathcal{H}_{\phi} needs to double the resolution of the input latent 𝐳 0 r \mathbf{z}_{0}^{r} . While we could use any super-resolution backbone with an adjusted number of input/output channels and train on paired data, this would require the model to learn spatial upsampling behavior in the latent space from scratch. Instead, we reuse the first decoding block of the VAE decoder, denoted as 𝒟 ( 1 ) \mathcal{D}^{(1)} , which already implements latent upsampling and has been well trained on massive data. This pretrained block serves as a spatial prior , effectively guiding ℋ ϕ \mathcal{H}_{\phi} ’s spatial upsampling operation. However, this block often produces feature maps with a different number of channels and unaligned geometry compared to the desired output 𝐳 0 4 ​ r \mathbf{z}_{0}^{4r} . Hence, we need a projection head to adjust the number of channels and refine the geometry of the produced latent output. In summary, our proposed Latent Hyperloop ℋ ϕ \mathcal{H}_{\phi} consists of two components: a frozen VAE decoding block 𝒟 ( 1 ) \mathcal{D}^{(1)} and a trainable projection head h ψ h_{\psi} . Because context-expanded patching uses an input crop larger than the coordinate-matched source region, the spatial size entering ℋ ϕ \mathcal{H}_{\phi} is larger than the nominal source patch size. We therefore adjust the padding in 𝒟 ( 1 ) \mathcal{D}^{(1)} and the early layers of h ψ h_{\psi} so that the output matches the required target patch size, requiring no major architectural change. Our data construction avoids that flaw, allowing UltraFlash to even surpass the original cascade baseline with VAE round trip in terms of quality, as will be shown in Section 5 . Training Objectives. After constructing training data, we define training losses for building a high-quality Latent Hyperloop ℋ ϕ \mathcal{H}_{\phi} . A straightforward objective is latent reconstruction, implemented by an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} reconstruction loss: ℒ r ​ e ​ c = ‖ 𝐳 o ​ u ​ t − 𝐳 ^ o ​ u ​ t ‖ 1 . \mathcal{L}_{rec}=\|\mathbf{z}^{out}-\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{out}\|_{1}. (5) While ℓ 2 \ell_{2} is a common choice, it is less effective for latent-space reconstruction, as noted in recent works ( Lin et al., 2024a ; Zhang and Hooi, 2023 ; Nguyen et al., 2025 ) . The ℓ 1 \ell_{1} objective provides better training stability and preserves the structural sparsity of the upsampled latent. Attention Alignment ( ℒ a ​ t ​ t ​ e ​ n \mathcal{L}_{atten} ). Reconstruction loss alone is insufficient. Since the loss is operated directly on the latent manifold, a small numerical distance error does not necessarily guarantee that two latents are perceptually or semantically equivalent. Furthermore, by treating each latent pixel independently, a simple reconstruction objective often tolerates subtle misalignments. Both lead to a loss of fine-grained structure in the decoded image. sections.heading: 4.2 Sparse Patch-based Decoding: Accelerating Final RGB Decoding
sections.text: While Latent Hyperloop removes avoidable intermediate RGB round trips, the final pixel-space transition is unavoidable: after refinement, the latent 𝐳 0 R \mathbf{z}_{0}^{R} must be decoded into RGB. At megapixel scale, however, full-latent VAE decoding is often memory-prohibitive, so practical synthesis pipelines decode the latent patch by patch and blend overlapping regions ( Bar-Tal et al., 2023 ; Du et al., 2024 ; Vontobel et al., 2025 ; Lai et al., 2026 ) . Dense overlap helps suppress seams, but it also repeats VAE computation over many regions. A natural acceleration is to reduce the overlap, but naive sparse decoding introduces visible boundary artifacts, including color shifts, brightness inconsistencies, and texture discontinuities at patch boundaries, as shown in Fig. 3 . Figure 3: Shared GroupNorm statistics enable sparse final RGB decoding. When overlap is small, standard patch-wise decoding shows seam artifacts caused by independently computed GroupNorm statistics. Sparse Patch-based Decoding uses shared cached statistics to align normalization across patches, making adjacent patches decode consistently. The right plot shows that our method maintains consistently low boundary MSE across overlap factors when decoding with sparse overlaps. Why Sparse Decoding Fails. We trace the root cause of sparse-decoding artifacts to the GroupNorm (GN) layers in the VAE decoder. GroupNorm ( Wu and He, 2018 ) normalizes activations within each group of channels using statistics computed from the current input. When the full image is decoded in a single pass, the mean μ \mu and variance σ 2 \sigma^{2} are computed over the entire spatial extent, producing globally consistent normalization. However, when decoding individual patches, each patch computes its own μ ( j ) \mu^{(j)} and σ 2 ​ ( j ) \sigma^{2(j)} based only on its local spatial content. Patches with different spatial content ( e.g. , a bright sky vs. a dark ground) yield substantially different statistics. This causes the same latent values in overlapping regions to be decoded to different pixel values depending on which patch they belong to, producing visible seams even after blending. Shared GN Statistics. Our solution is simple and requires no training. We compute a set of reference GroupNorm statistics once, then reuse them for all patches during decoding. First, we decode a set of reference patches { P ref ( i ) } i = 1 N ref \{P_{\mathrm{ref}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{ref}}} (utilizing the four corner patches of the latent) through the VAE decoder, recording the GroupNorm statistics ( μ l ref , σ l ref ) (\mu_{l}^{\mathrm{ref}},\sigma_{l}^{\mathrm{ref}}) at every layer l l . The cached statistics are 𝒞 = { ( μ l ref , σ l ref ) } l = 1 L \mathcal{C}=\{(\mu_{l}^{\mathrm{ref}},\sigma_{l}^{\mathrm{ref}})\}_{l=1}^{L} , where L L is the number of GroupNorm layers in the VAE decoder. Second, when decoding each patch P ( j ) P^{(j)} , we replace the per-patch GroupNorm computation with the cached reference statistics. This ensures that identical latent values always produce identical pixel values, regardless of which patch they belong to. The overlapping regions now agree perfectly, and simple blending, or even direct stitching, produces seamless results. Enabling Smaller Overlap. A key benefit of Sparse Patch-based Decoding is that it enables the use of much smaller overlaps during patch-wise VAE decoding. In standard cascade and patch-based synthesis pipelines ( Bar-Tal et al., 2023 ; Du et al., 2024 ; Vontobel et al., 2025 ; Lai et al., 2026 ) , large overlaps (e.g., 25%) are often needed to mask patch-boundary inconsistencies through blending. With cached GroupNorm statistics, the overlap can be reduced by up to 8 × \times in our main setting while preserving visual continuity, since it no longer needs to hide per-patch normalization mismatch. This directly translates to fewer total patches and faster decoding: N patches = ⌈ H − o H p − o ⌉ × ⌈ W − o W p − o ⌉ , N_{\mathrm{patches}}=\left\lceil\frac{H-o}{H_{p}-o}\right\rceil\times\left\lceil\frac{W-o}{W_{p}-o}\right\rceil, (8) where H p × W p H_{p}\times W_{p} is the patch size and o o is the overlap. Smaller overlap increases the patch stride and reduces N patches N_{\mathrm{patches}} ; in our main 4K setting, this reduces the number of decoded patches by up to 30–40% , leading to a proportional reduction in VAE decoding time. Fig. 3 quantifies boundary consistency across overlap settings. We vary the overlap factor and measure the MSE between decoded pixel values in overlapping regions of adjacent patches, averaged over 100 held-out latents. Standard decoding exhibits high boundary error that decreases only gradually with larger overlaps, while Sparse Patch-based Decoding maintains low boundary error by enforcing globally consistent GroupNorm statistics.

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Settings
sections.text: Latent Hyperloop. Latent Hyperloop is a lightweight network with ∼ 5 \sim 5 M trainable parameters. Unless otherwise stated, we use SwinIR ( Liang et al., 2021 ) as the projection head backbone and train it with the objectives described in Sec. 4.1 . For the attention-alignment loss, we use a fixed noising level t = 1 t=1 and temperature τ = 3.0 \tau=3.0 . Training data consists of 1.2M images synthesized with SDXL ( Podell et al., 2023 ) using prompts from JourneyDB ( Sun et al., 2024 ) and LAION ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) , each paired with its 2 × 2\times -interpolated version as described in Sec. 4.1 . Training uses 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs (80GB each) with a batch size of 32 per GPU, i.e., a global batch size of 256; optimization details are given in Appendix A.3 . Evaluation Data and Metrics. Following prior protocols ( Du et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ) , we evaluate on 1000 prompts sampled from LAION-Aesthetics ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ; Schuhmann, 2022 ) and report Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) , crop-based FID (FID c ), Inception Score (IS) ( Salimans et al., 2016 ) , and wall-clock inference time. FID measures global distribution quality, while FID c evaluates local high-frequency fidelity using crops without resizing. All latency numbers are measured on a single NVIDIA A100-40GB GPU unless stated otherwise. Baselines. Our main comparison focuses on SDXL-based cascade methods, including FouriScale ( Huang et al., 2024 ) , DemoFusion ( Du et al., 2024 ) , FreeScale ( Qiu et al., 2025 ) , and the fast cascade baseline PixelRush ( Lai et al., 2026 ) . This setting provides a direct comparison because these methods share a similar base-model regime and target high-resolution extrapolation from pretrained native-resolution generators. We use PixelRush as the representative fast cascade pipeline because it offers the strongest speed–quality trade-off among prior cascade methods. Unlike FouriScale, DemoFusion, and FreeScale, which rely on multi-step SDXL refinement, PixelRush uses one-step Turbo refinement for rapid generation. We denote configurations by the refiner used in the cascade: -SD uses SD-Turbo, while -XL uses SDXL-Turbo ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) . Unless otherwise specified, both configurations follow the same base-generation protocol. Finally, UltraFlash denotes the PixelRush fast cascade equipped with our Latent Hyperloop and Sparse Patch-based Decoding. Refinement-stage sparse patching. PixelRush already uses sparse patching during diffusion refinement to reduce overlap between refinement patches, discussed in its supplemental materials. We regard this as part of the baseline cascade pipeline. It is separate from Sparse Patch-based Decoding : the former reduces denoising/refinement cost, while the latter reduces final VAE-to-RGB decoding cost by enabling small-overlap patch decoding without boundary artifacts. For fair comparison, we report PixelRush under the same refinement-stage sparse patching setting.

sections.heading: 5.3 Qualitative Comparison
sections.text: As illustrated in Fig. 4 , UltraFlash demonstrates superior structural coherence and realism compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. While baselines like FouriScale and DemoFusion exhibit structural deterioration at high resolutions (e.g., object repetition or unnatural texture), both PixelRush and UltraFlash maintain robust global layout. However, the advantage of UltraFlash becomes evident in the fine-grained details. As shown in the zoomed crops, our pipeline resolves sharper high-frequency textures, effectively mitigating the subtle smoothing artifacts observed in PixelRush.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented UltraFlash, a transition-efficient method for megapixel visual synthesis. Instead of only accelerating denoising, UltraFlash targets VAE-heavy pixel-space transitions in cascade pipelines. Latent Hyperloop replaces the intermediate decode–resize–encode round trip with a learned latent shortcut, while Sparse Patch-based Decoding accelerates final RGB reconstruction by sharing cached GroupNorm statistics across patches. Integrated into a state-of-the-art cascade baseline, UltraFlash reduces 4K latency by 2 × 2\times while improving image quality, showing that pixel-space transitions are an effective target for improving the speed–quality trade-off of megapixel synthesis.

sections.heading: A.1 Implementation Details
sections.text: Base Generation. Following previous works, we use SDXL as the default base model to generate images at its native 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 resolution with a classifier-free guidance scale of 7.5. The reverse diffusion process uses deterministic DDIM sampling ( η = 0 \eta=0 ). Cascade Upsampling. Our pipeline operates in a cascaded manner, doubling the spatial resolution at each level. For example, generating an 8192 × 8192 8192\times 8192 image proceeds as 1024 → 2048 → 4096 → 8192 1024\to 2048\to 4096\to 8192 , with refinement applied at each level. At each cascade level, the Latent Hyperloop adapter upsamples the latent by 2 × 2\times . Since the adapter backbone is lightweight ( ∼ \sim 4.8M parameters), the computational overhead of processing overlapping regions is negligible, so we use a generous 50% overlap for the upsampling stage to ensure smooth transitions. Patch Extraction. For the refinement stage, we support two patching strategies. In dense patching , the upsampled latent is tiled into patches with 50% overlap along both spatial dimensions. In sparse patching , we reduce the total number of patches for faster inference. Given the target number of patches per row (or column) as e e , the fixed patch window size w w , and the upsampling factor relative to the original patch window size u u , we need to compute the overlap size for interior patches o o and the last patch o last o_{\mathrm{last}} that satisfy: o ⋅ ( e − 2 ) + o last = ( e − u ) ⋅ w o\cdot(e-2)+o_{\mathrm{last}}=(e-u)\cdot w (A1) To distribute the overlaps almost evenly, we compute them as follows: o \displaystyle o = ⌊ ( e − u ) ⋅ w e − 1 ⌋ , \displaystyle=\lfloor\frac{(e-u)\cdot w}{e-1}\rfloor, (A2) o last \displaystyle o_{\mathrm{last}} = ( e − u ) ⋅ w − o ⋅ ( e − 2 ) \displaystyle=(e-u)\cdot w-o\cdot(e-2) (A3) Table A1 summarizes the patching configurations. At 8 × 8\times the window size (e.g., SD-Turbo at 4K), the reduction is more substantial: 11 patches per row/column versus 15 with dense patching. Note that SDXL-Turbo at 2K cannot benefit from sparse patching, as dense patching already produces only 3 patches along each dimension, which is the minimum needed for full coverage. sections.heading: A.3 Latent Hyperloop
sections.text: We adopt a SwinIR-based architecture for the Latent Hyperloop (LH) and incorporate structural priors from the VAE decoder to guide the learned upsampling. With SDXL-Turbo refiner, LH accepts latent patch inputs with resolution 80 × 80 80\times 80 , i.e., a 64 × 64 64\times 64 source crop expanded by p = 8 p=8 context pixels on each side (input side length s + 2 ​ p s+2p with s = 64 s=64 ), to generate upsampled latent patches with resolution 128 × 128 128\times 128 . With SD-Turbo, while we could use smaller input and output patch sizes to align with SD-Turbo’s convention, we find it unnecessary and use the same config as with SDXL-Turbo ( 80 × 80 80\times 80 for input and 128 × 128 128\times 128 for output) for simple implementation. The model is trained from scratch using the AdamW optimizer with a fixed learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} (no scheduling) for 20K steps on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs (80GB each), with a batch size of 32 per GPU (global batch size 256).

sections.heading: A.4 Sparse VAE Decoding
sections.text: Overview. When decoding a high-resolution latent (spatial dimensions ≥ 512 \geq 512 ), a single-pass VAE decode causes out-of-memory errors. The standard solution is patch-wise decoding with overlapping regions. Large overlaps produce seamless results but are slow. Our Sparse VAE Decoding enables small overlaps by ensuring consistent GroupNorm statistics across all patches. CrossPatchGroupNorm. We replace every GroupNorm layer in the VAE decoder with a custom CrossPatchGroupNorm module that can operate in two modes: (1) standard mode, computing statistics from the current input, and (2) cached mode, using pre-computed reference statistics. Reference statistics from the first batch. Rather than requiring a separate reference pass, we compute and cache GroupNorm statistics from the first batch of patches. During the first batch’s forward pass, a forward hook on each CrossPatchGroupNorm layer records the mean and variance aggregated over both the batch and spatial dimensions: μ l ref = 1 B ⋅ | 𝒮 | ​ ∑ b , s 𝐡 l ( b , s ) , σ l 2 , ref = 1 B ⋅ | 𝒮 | ​ ∑ b , s ( 𝐡 l ( b , s ) − μ l ref ) 2 , \mu_{l}^{\mathrm{ref}}=\frac{1}{B\cdot|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{b,s}\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(b,s)},\quad\sigma_{l}^{2,\mathrm{ref}}=\frac{1}{B\cdot|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{b,s}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{(b,s)}-\mu_{l}^{\mathrm{ref}})^{2}, (A4) where B B is the batch size and 𝒮 \mathcal{S} denotes the spatial and channel-group dimensions. After the first batch completes, the hooks are removed and all subsequent batches use the cached statistics automatically. Batched decoding. Patches of standard size are grouped into mini-batches and decoded in parallel. Edge patches with non-standard sizes (at image boundaries) are decoded individually with cached statistics. After all patches are decoded, adjacent patches are blended along both vertical and horizontal directions to produce the final seamless output. sections.text: InvSR 1 1 1 Z. Yue, K. Liao, and C. C. Loy, “Arbitrary-steps image super-resolution via diffusion inversion,” in CVPR , pp. 23153–23163, 2025. is a pretrained model for diffusion inversion, targeting the super-resolution task. It takes a coarsely upsampled latent as input and predicts its noise residual, which is added to the input latent to form the noisy latent to produce the super-resolution outcome via one diffusion forward step. This formulation is naturally compatible with our refinement stage: we can introduce a parallel InvSR branch alongside the existing DDIM inversion branch, blending their outputs to combine the structural fidelity of DDIM inversion with the detail-aware noise prediction of InvSR. Specifically, we compute both the DDIM-inverted noise 𝐳 ¯ K DDIM \bar{\mathbf{z}}_{K}^{\mathrm{DDIM}} and the InvSR-predicted noise 𝐳 ¯ K InvSR \bar{\mathbf{z}}_{K}^{\mathrm{InvSR}} , then combine them via spherical linear interpolation (Slerp): 𝐳 K = Slerp ⁡ ( 𝐳 ¯ K DDIM , 𝐳 ¯ K InvSR , α ) , α = 0.8 , \mathbf{z}_{K}=\mathrm{Slerp}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{K}^{\mathrm{DDIM}},\;\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{K}^{\mathrm{InvSR}},\;\alpha),\quad\alpha=0.8, (A5) where α = 0.8 \alpha=0.8 assigns the dominant weight to DDIM inversion. We use Slerp rather than linear interpolation because noisy latents in diffusion models lie on a high-dimensional hypersphere, and Slerp preserves the norm and angular distribution of the interpolated noise. Table A2 shows that InvSR alone does not provide strong scores when generating high-resolution images. However, it is highly compatible with our pipeline, and incorporating InvSR into UltraFlash consistently improves both FID and IS across resolutions. These gains come at the cost of one additional InvSR forward pass per patch, which adds moderate overhead but can be worthwhile when quality is prioritized over speed. sections.heading: C.2 Effect of Training Objectives on Latent Hyperloop Reconstruction
sections.text: Fig. A4 provides a qualitative comparison of the training objectives used for learning the Latent Hyperloop adapter. Using only the ℓ 1 \ell_{1} reconstruction loss preserves the coarse object layout, but the reconstructed image remains visibly over-smoothed, with weakened local contrast and softened facial structure. Adding E-LatentLPIPS yields only limited perceptual improvement over ℓ 1 \ell_{1} alone. In contrast, incorporating the proposed Attention Alignment objective produces substantially sharper and more faithful reconstructions, especially in fine-grained regions such as the eyes, nose contour, and surrounding fur. These visual differences support the design choice of using Attention Alignment to improve latent-space upsampling quality. From left to right: reconstructions trained with ℓ 1 \ell_{1} only, ℓ 1 \ell_{1} + E-LatentLPIPS, and ℓ 1 \ell_{1} + Attention Alignment, followed by the ground-truth reconstruction. All variants use the same latent upsampling backbone and are trained under the same setting. While ℓ 1 \ell_{1} preserves the overall structure, it produces noticeably smooth reconstructions, and E-LatentLPIPS provides only marginal visual improvement. The proposed Attention Alignment objective better preserves local structure and fine facial details, yielding reconstructions that are visually closest to the ground truth. Best viewed zoomed in.

sections.heading: Appendix D Limitations
sections.text: UltraFlash is developed and evaluated for cascade-based megapixel image synthesis. This focus allows us to isolate and optimize a concrete bottleneck that appears in practical high-resolution text-to-image pipelines: VAE-heavy transitions between latent and pixel space. We therefore view the method as a targeted acceleration strategy for image synthesis rather than a claim about all generative settings. Other modalities, such as video generation, introduce additional temporal and architectural considerations that are outside the scope of this work. At the same time, the central observation behind UltraFlash is broader: as denoising becomes faster, the surrounding transition costs become increasingly important. Exploring transition-aware acceleration beyond image cascades is a natural direction for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix E Broader Impact
sections.text: UltraFlash improves the efficiency of high-resolution image synthesis by reducing transition overhead in cascade pipelines. This can make megapixel generation more practical for creative tools, design workflows, data visualization, and research settings where high-resolution outputs are useful but computational cost is a barrier. At the same time, faster and higher-resolution generation should be deployed with the same safeguards used for the underlying generative models, including content filtering, provenance or watermarking mechanisms when available, and responsible-use policies. UltraFlash does not introduce a new generative prior or bypass the safety behavior of the base models; it accelerates the transition operations around existing cascade refinement. We therefore view its impact as primarily improving efficiency, while inheriting the broader benefits and risks of the image-generation systems on which it is built.

Anh Nguyen 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Phong Nguyen Anh Tran Affiliation: Qualcomm AI Research Abstract Megapixel visual synthesis with latent diffusion models requires operating far beyond the resolution at which these models are trained. Cascade refinement is the most successful approach to handling this problem: it upgrades a base image at a regular resolution to the target resolution via multiple cascade upsampling steps, each involving a resolution upgrade traversed through pixel space and a denoising-based refinement in latent space. Although denoising is often treated as the main cost, we identify an underexplored source of overhead: repeatedly moving representations through the VAE. We refer to these steps as pixel-space transitions : intermediate latents are decoded to RGB, resized, and re-encoded before refinement, while final latents are decoded patch by patch with dense overlap to suppress artifacts. We present UltraFlash , which shifts the focus of acceleration from denoising alone to the VAE transitions around it. Its first component, Latent Hyperloop , replaces the intermediate RGB round trip with a learned latent-space shortcut that approximates the same transformation while avoiding repeated VAE calls for decoding and encoding. Its second component, Sparse Patch-based Decoding , makes final reconstruction efficient by tracing patch seams to inconsistent GroupNorm statistics and reusing cached statistics across patches, enabling sparse VAE decoding with much smaller overlap. Integrated into the current state-of-the-art baseline, UltraFlash reduces 4K generation latency by ∼ \sim 2 × \times while improving image quality, demonstrating that transition-level optimization can advance both efficiency and fidelity. More broadly, these transition costs recur across megapixel synthesis pipelines, suggesting that optimizing pixel-space transitions is an effective route to fast, high-fidelity visual synthesis. Figure 1: UltraFlash improves the 4K speed–quality frontier. It achieves a 2 × 2\times speedup over the current state-of-the-art cascade baseline with better FID, moving closer to the Pareto-optimal frontier. 1 Introduction Latent diffusion models have greatly advanced visual synthesis, but their native training resolution remains a practical boundary. Although applications increasingly require 2K, 4K, and larger outputs, models trained around 512 × 512 512\times 512 or 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 often produce repeated objects, distorted layouts, or unstable textures when directly evaluated on larger canvases. Fine-tuning on high-resolution data is a natural remedy, but it is difficult to scale: diverse megapixel-scale datasets are limited, training at such resolutions is expensive, and the adapted model often becomes specialized to a fixed target resolution ( Xie et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . Existing alternatives therefore rely on inference-time strategies that reuse pretrained models. Direct extrapolation methods modify inference on enlarged latents, but can suffer from memory cost and structural instability at extreme resolutions. Cascade refinement methods instead generate at a reliable native resolution and progressively construct larger images through refinement stages ( Du et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ; Vontobel et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) . Representative systems differ in how they refine enlarged latents: DemoFusion uses progressive patch-based refinement, FouriScale and FreeScale modify frequency or scale behavior, HiWave uses structure-preserving inversion, and PixelRush ( Lai et al., 2026 ) accelerates the cascade with one-step diffusion refinement. Among these, PixelRush currently provides the strongest speed–quality trade-off, making it the most relevant stress test for remaining non-denoising overhead. We therefore use PixelRush as the main instantiation of UltraFlash, while targeting VAE-heavy pixel-space transitions that are shared by the broader cascade family. Most acceleration efforts for megapixel synthesis focus on denoising or refinement. This is natural, since diffusion sampling is expensive and larger spatial sizes increase the cost of each denoising operation. However, we find that this view is incomplete. Modern cascade pipelines also spend substantial time repeatedly moving representations through the VAE. We call these operations pixel-space transitions : steps where a latent representation is converted to RGB or where RGB is converted back to a latent representation. These transitions appear in two places. First, intermediate latents are often decoded to RGB, resized, and re-encoded before refinement. Second, the final latent must be decoded to RGB, but at megapixel scale this is typically done patch by patch with dense overlap to suppress artifacts. As a result, a significant fraction of runtime is spent not on denoising itself, but on VAE-heavy transitions around denoising. This observation exposes an underexplored source of overhead. The two transitions have different roles and therefore require different solutions. The intermediate RGB round trip is avoidable: it is used as a convenient way to transform a latent before refinement, but it need not be performed through pixels. The final transition is unavoidable because the output image must be RGB, but its dense patch implementation is inefficient. Thus, the design goal is to replace the avoidable intermediate VAE round trip and make the final VAE decoding sparse without introducing seams. We present UltraFlash , which shifts the focus of acceleration from denoising alone to the VAE transitions around it. UltraFlashcontains two components. First, Latent Hyperloop replaces the intermediate RGB round trip with a learned latent-space shortcut. It approximates the decode–resize–encode transformation while avoiding repeated VAE calls for decoding and encoding. Second, Sparse Patch-based Decoding accelerates final reconstruction. We trace sparse patch-decoding artifacts to inconsistent GroupNorm statistics across independently decoded patches. Sparse Patch-based Decoding fixes this by caching normalization statistics from reference patches and reusing them across all patches, enabling sparse VAE decoding with much smaller overlap. Integrated into the current state-of-the-art cascade baseline ( Lai et al., 2026 ) , UltraFlash reduces 4K generation latency by 2 × 2\times while improving image quality. This result shows that VAE transitions remain a substantial optimization spot even in highly optimized megapixel synthesis systems. More broadly, RGB round trips and dense patch-wise VAE decoding appear across cascade pipelines, suggesting that optimizing pixel-space transitions is an effective route to faster, high-fidelity visual synthesis. Our contributions are: • We identify repeated VAE-heavy pixel-space transitions as an underexplored source of overhead in megapixel visual synthesis, beyond denoising and refinement. • We introduce Latent Hyperloop , a learned latent-space shortcut that replaces the intermediate decode–resize–encode round trip while avoiding repeated VAE decoding and encoding. • We introduce Sparse Patch-based Decoding , which enables sparse VAE decoding by sharing cached normalization statistics across independently decoded patches. 2 Related Work Megapixel Visual Synthesis. Scaling diffusion models beyond their native training resolution has been explored through several routes. One route trains or adapts models for native high-resolution generation, such as SANA, HunyuanImage, and other dedicated 2K/4K generators ( Xie et al., 2025 ; Team, 2025 ) . These methods can achieve strong quality, but they require high-resolution data, model adaptation, or dedicated training. A second route directly extrapolates pretrained models to larger canvases through inference-time modifications, such as convolutional dilation ( He et al., 2023 ) , frequency or scale fusion ( Huang et al., 2024 ) , flow-aligned guidance ( Bu et al., 2025 ) , or positional extrapolation for FLUX-based models ( Issachar et al., 2025 ) . These methods avoid retraining, but can suffer from memory cost, structural instability, or unnatural textures at extreme resolutions ( Lin et al., 2024b ) . A third route uses cascade or region-based refinement, synthesizing native-resolution windows and merging them into a larger image through average blending ( Bar-Tal et al., 2023 ; Du et al., 2024 ) , DDIM inversion ( Vontobel et al., 2025 ) , or few-step refinement ( Lai et al., 2026 ) . This cascade line has progressed from multi-step patch refinement in DemoFusion to structure-preserving inversion in HiWave, and most recently to PixelRush, which uses one-step Turbo refinement to deliver the strongest speed–quality trade-off among cascade methods. Our work focuses on the cascade setting because it reuses pretrained models in their reliable operating regime while supporting megapixel outputs. We use PixelRush as the main experimental instantiation because it is already optimized for denoising speed; improving it therefore tests whether VAE transition overhead remains a meaningful bottleneck after the dominant sampling cost has been compressed. Rather than introducing another refinement strategy, UltraFlash optimizes the VAE-heavy transitions surrounding refinement: intermediate RGB round trips that prepare refinement inputs, and final patch-wise VAE decoding that reconstructs the output image. Pixel-Space Transitions. Latent diffusion models use a VAE to move between compressed latents and RGB images ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . In megapixel synthesis, this creates two transition costs. First, intermediate latents are often decoded to RGB, resized, and re-encoded before refinement. This route is stable and avoids artifacts from naive latent manipulation ( Qiu et al., 2025 ; Vontobel et al., 2025 ) , but requires an expensive decode–encode round trip. Because the VAE encoder is nonlinear, ordinary latent interpolation is not that round trip. FAM Diffusion ( Yang et al., 2025 ) compensates with learned frequency and attention modulation over the whole latent, and it changes the denoiser. Latent Hyperloop is a patch-wise shortcut for the same decode–resize–encode transformation and leaves the denoiser unchanged. Second, the final latent must be decoded to RGB. Since full-image VAE decoding is memory-intensive at megapixel scale, pipelines decode overlapping patches and blend them. Large overlaps hide seams but repeat computation; small overlaps reveal boundary artifacts. We identify inconsistent GroupNorm statistics ( Wu and He, 2018 ) across patches as a key cause, and use Sparse Patch-based Decoding to share cached statistics across patches, enabling sparse reconstruction with much smaller overlap. Super-Resolution. Super-resolution methods reconstruct high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs ( Chen et al., 2024b ; Dong et al., 2014 ; Wang et al., 2020 ) . Diffusion-based super-resolution methods ( Li et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) further improve perceptual quality, but are typically trained for restoration. Megapixel visual synthesis differs from restoration: the input is a generated intermediate representation, and the goal is coherent visual synthesis rather than recovering a unique high-resolution target ( Lai et al., 2026 ) . Thus, although super-resolution and megapixel synthesis both involve scale expansion, they address different problem settings and require different evaluation criteria. 3 Background Latent Diffusion Models ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) perform diffusion in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder. At megapixel scale, however, full-latent VAE decoding is often memory-prohibitive, so practical synthesis pipelines decode the latent patch by patch and blend overlapping regions ( Bar-Tal et al., 2023 ; Du et al., 2024 ; Vontobel et al., 2025 ; Lai et al., 2026 ) . Dense overlap helps suppress seams, but it also repeats VAE computation over many regions. A natural acceleration is to reduce the overlap, but naive sparse decoding introduces visible boundary artifacts, including color shifts, brightness inconsistencies, and texture discontinuities at patch boundaries, as shown in Fig. 3 . Figure 3: Shared GroupNorm statistics enable sparse final RGB decoding. When overlap is small, standard patch-wise decoding shows seam artifacts caused by independently computed GroupNorm statistics. The right plot shows that our method maintains consistently low boundary MSE across overlap factors when decoding with sparse overlaps. Why Sparse Decoding Fails. We trace the root cause of sparse-decoding artifacts to the GroupNorm (GN) layers in the VAE decoder. GroupNorm ( Wu and He, 2018 ) normalizes activations within each group of channels using statistics computed from the current input. When the full image is decoded in a single pass, the mean μ \mu and variance σ 2 \sigma^{2} are computed over the entire spatial extent, producing globally consistent normalization. However, when decoding individual patches, each patch computes its own μ ( j ) \mu^{(j)} and σ 2 ​ ( j ) \sigma^{2(j)} based only on its local spatial content. Patches with different spatial content ( e.g. , a bright sky vs. a dark ground) yield substantially different statistics. This causes the same latent values in overlapping regions to be decoded to different pixel values depending on which patch they belong to, producing visible seams even after blending. Shared GN Statistics. Our solution is simple and requires no training. We compute a set of reference GroupNorm statistics once, then reuse them for all patches during decoding. First, we decode a set of reference patches { P ref ( i ) } i = 1 N ref \{P_{\mathrm{ref}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{ref}}} (utilizing the four corner patches of the latent) through the VAE decoder, recording the GroupNorm statistics ( μ l ref , σ l ref ) (\mu_{l}^{\mathrm{ref}},\sigma_{l}^{\mathrm{ref}}) at every layer l l . The cached statistics are 𝒞 = { ( μ l ref , σ l ref ) } l = 1 L \mathcal{C}=\{(\mu_{l}^{\mathrm{ref}},\sigma_{l}^{\mathrm{ref}})\}_{l=1}^{L} , where L L is the number of GroupNorm layers in the VAE decoder. Second, when decoding each patch P ( j ) P^{(j)} , we replace the per-patch GroupNorm computation with the cached reference statistics. This ensures that identical latent values always produce identical pixel values, regardless of which patch they belong to. The overlapping regions now agree perfectly, and simple blending, or even direct stitching, produces seamless results. Enabling Smaller Overlap. A key benefit of Sparse Patch-based Decoding is that it enables the use of much smaller overlaps during patch-wise VAE decoding. In standard cascade and patch-based synthesis pipelines ( Bar-Tal et al., 2023 ; Du et al., 2024 ; Vontobel et al., 2025 ; Lai et al., 2026 ) , large overlaps (e.g., 25%) are often needed to mask patch-boundary inconsistencies through blending. Latent Hyperloop is a lightweight network with ∼ 5 \sim 5 M trainable parameters. Unless otherwise stated, we use SwinIR ( Liang et al., 2021 ) as the projection head backbone and train it with the objectives described in Sec. 4.1 . For the attention-alignment loss, we use a fixed noising level t = 1 t=1 and temperature τ = 3.0 \tau=3.0 . Training data consists of 1.2M images synthesized with SDXL ( Podell et al., 2023 ) using prompts from JourneyDB ( Sun et al., 2024 ) and LAION ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) , each paired with its 2 × 2\times -interpolated version as described in Sec. 4.1 . Training uses 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs (80GB each) with a batch size of 32 per GPU, i.e., a global batch size of 256; optimization details are given in Appendix A.3 . Evaluation Data and Metrics. Following prior protocols ( Du et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ) , we evaluate on 1000 prompts sampled from LAION-Aesthetics ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ; Schuhmann, 2022 ) and report Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) , crop-based FID (FID c ), Inception Score (IS) ( Salimans et al., 2016 ) , and wall-clock inference time. All latency numbers are measured on a single NVIDIA A100-40GB GPU unless stated otherwise. Baselines. This setting provides a direct comparison because these methods share a similar base-model regime and target high-resolution extrapolation from pretrained native-resolution generators.
